surfaces.rationale: AES-128 and AES-256 remain future first-party implementations with architecture-specific review gates.
GHASH and AES-GCM remain future bounded AEAD work with nonce and counter exhaustion enforcement.
ChaCha20 remains separate first-party work with checked block counters and deterministic exhaustion closure.
ChaCha20, Poly1305, and their AEAD composition remain staged first-party future work.
Concrete ECDHE-ML-KEM groups remain blocked pending both final Standards Track text and final IANA values.
Ed25519 remains future strict verification and signing work with canonical encoding checks.
P-256, P-384, X25519, ECDSA, and ECDH depend on reviewed fixed-limb field and group operations.
GHASH finite-field arithmetic remains separate constant-time work with bounded incremental processing and full-width proof obligations.
HKDF remains future first-party extract and expand logic with bounded labels and outputs.
HMAC-SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-384 remain future first-party constant-time constructions.
Legacy PKCS1 client CertificateVerify signature code points are excluded from TLS 1.3 version one.
ML-KEM remains future first-party key-establishment work subject to FIPS 203 and transition policy.
RSA-PSS verification and bounded RSA arithmetic remain future work before any private operation.
SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 remain staged first-party implementations with known-answer, boundary, and differential evidence.
Keccak-f[1600], SHA3-256, SHA3-512, SHAKE128, and SHAKE256 remain staged first-party work under the pinned current FIPS 202 authority.
Opaque caller-provided path tokens bind cookie, amplification, CID, migration, PMTU, timer, and datagram state without address interpretation.
The optional CRYPTO-offset reassembly helper is explicit, bounded, conflict-detecting, and never implements retransmission or loss recovery.
Brynja consumes ordered CRYPTO bytes and emits secret events while packet numbers, retransmission, loss, Retry, key phase, and transport remain caller-owned.
TLS emits typed traffic secrets and an optional helper derives QUIC keys while Initial salts, packet protection, Retry, and key phase stay in transport.
Transport parameters receive bounded syntactic parsing and transcript binding while all transport-semantic enforcement remains caller-owned.
Certificate decompression remains hostile pre-authentication work behind a caller-owned bounded receive provider.
Precompressed certificate artifacts require bounded decompression, canonical byte comparison, complete input binding, and rotation invalidation.
Certificate compression sending requires peer negotiation, current validated artifacts, exact transcript bytes, and fail-closed fallback policy.
The selected SP 800-90A DRBG requires complete instantiate, generate, reseed, uninstantiate, state-protection, and catastrophic-error behavior.
The selected SP 800-90C RBG construction requires exact source and DRBG topology, reseed chains, health propagation, and service boundaries.
Secure-random contracts require explicit caller and provider duties without implying that an arbitrary random source is validated entropy.
FIPS entropy-source admission requires exact construction, operational environment, assessment, health tests, and catastrophic failure handling.
Certificate authentication combined with an external PSK is excluded from version one.
Heartbeat negotiation and content are rejected in every modern TLS and DTLS profile.
Record Size Limit requires directional negotiation, fragmentation and buffering limits, peer-violation handling, and interoperability evidence.
Local configuration cannot enable, offer, echo, or negotiate unsupported RFC 6066 facilities even though bounded peer ClientHello inputs are safely ignored.
Production SSLKEYLOGFILE export is forbidden because it defeats the secret-lifetime contract.
Key logging may exist only in separately compiled repository test support that cannot enter production packages.
status_request_v2 is excluded from the hardened TLS 1.2 version-one profile.
TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication is excluded from the version-one state machine.
Unknown ignorable extension values are preserved only where the governing protocol explicitly permits safe ignore.
Delegated credentials require strict lifetime, algorithm, transcript, and certificate binding.
ML-KEM PKIX credentials are excluded; ML-KEM is admitted only for explicitly approved key establishment.
PEM and certificate-chain containers require bounded decoding and exact label handling.
PKCS8, SEC1, and PKCS1 private-key containers require bounded DER and strict algorithm binding.
Raw public keys remain an opt-in authentication profile separate from X.509 trust processing.
Signed X.509 certificates require bounded DER, algorithm consistency, path processing, and identity validation.
Unsigned X.509 certificates are excluded from the version-one authentication and trust model.

PCT remains blocked until authenticated protocol-source provenance and rights are recorded.
Secure Network Programming remains blocked until authenticated protocol-source provenance and rights are recorded.
SSL 1 reconstruction research remains source-blocked and can never become a secure or published protocol product.
SSL 2.0 remains source-blocked before any independent insecure legacy release line can begin.
SSL 3.0 is confined to an independently packaged insecure legacy release line and remains prohibited by current TLS policy.
TLS 1.0 is confined to an independently packaged insecure legacy release line.
TLS 1.1 is confined to an independently packaged insecure legacy release line.
WTLS research and implementation remain blocked until authenticated protocol-source provenance and rights are recorded.
Certificate Transparency validation remains explicitly versioned future work.
DTLS 1.2 remains a hardened compatibility profile isolated from the DTLS 1.3 engine.
DTLS 1.3 remains future work in its independent datagram state-machine boundary.
ECH remains future work with caller-owned DNS, retry, configuration generation, and inner-name policy.
ECH client construction requires exact inner and outer messages, AAD, padding, transcript preservation, GREASE, and resource policy.
ECH configuration bootstrap and cache lifecycle require bounded hostile parsing, typed provenance, mandatory-extension handling, expiry, and rotation.
ECH retry and rotation require exact HelloRetryRequest transcript invariants, retry authority, generation changes, and downgrade detection.
ECH server opening requires configuration lookup, uniform HPKE rejection, consistency checks, acceptance confirmation, and bound identity selection.
HPKE base mode is the only admitted mode and remains future bounded cryptographic work.
HPKE KEM and context derivation remain bounded cryptographic foundations downstream of validated provider ports.
HPKE export and context lifecycle require bounded output, role separation, exhaustion closure, cancellation, and immediate secret destruction.
HPKE authenticated and PSK modes are excluded from the version-one API and composition model.
OCSP parsing, validation, freshness, nonce, transport, and cache semantics remain staged future work.
QUIC v1 and v2 cryptography require distinct exact salts, labels, header protection, and version binding.
TLS 1.2 is retained only as a separately hardened compatibility engine with no downgrade path.
Current TLS 1.3 remains the primary future stream protocol and is not implemented by this release.
Path-bound cookies, amplification budgets, PMTU policy, and cheap rejection precede expensive cryptography and cannot transfer between paths.
DTLS requires loss, reorder, duplicate, fragmentation, replay, path, CID, version, load, fuzz, interoperability, and external-audit evidence.
Flights, ACKs, timer actions, retransmission caches, backoff, congestion, and path ownership are explicit, checked, and deterministic.
Handshake fragmentation and caller-workspace reassembly are bounded, transcript-canonical, duplicate-idempotent, and conflict-rejecting.
The DTLS router selects one highest acceptable engine once and never retries or crosses transcript, path, credential, ticket, epoch, replay, CID, or secret state.
Replay windows and epoch keys have fixed bounds, transactional installation, bounded retention, and immediate obsolete-key destruction.
Return-routability checks authenticate path challenge, response, timers, pacing, buffering, rebinding, migration, PMTU, and exact path binding.
DTLS negotiation skips unknown offers, rejects recognized legacy versions, selects one engine, and preserves transcript plus opaque path identity.
DTLS 1.2 CID negotiation preserves its version-specific record, routing, privacy, replay, migration, PMTU, and amplification invariants.
DTLS 1.2 uses only the hardened TLS 1.2 profile with isolated epoch, replay, ticket, path, downgrade, and deprecation state.
DTLS 1.3 CID updates bound active and retired identifiers and preserve collision, privacy, replay, routing, rotation, path, and amplification state.
DTLS 1.3 early data is never offered, accepted, derived, retained, or transcript-admitted, including reorder and duplicate cases.
DTLS 1.3 client and server states handle duplicates, key updates, terminal cleanup, provider cancellation, epochs, flights, and paths.
DTLS 1.3 unified headers, epochs, compact sequence reconstruction, nonce construction, and exhaustion are checked before state mutation.
Record-number encryption authenticates reconstruction and never mutates replay state before successful record authentication.
QUIC-TLS requires versioned vectors, loss and reorder simulation, discard, zero-RTT, derivation, interoperability, ownership, fuzz, and external review.
Tickets distinguish TLS completion from QUIC confirmation and bind QUIC version, parameters, ALPN, application, deployment, privacy, and rotation state.
The QUIC handshake has deterministic per-level input, output, alert, provider, future-data, secret-event, backpressure, and late-data behavior.
The recordless QUIC profile enforces encryption-level legality, required ALPN, secret events, and TLS-alert to CRYPTO_ERROR mapping.
QUIC zero-RTT enforces its sentinel size, remembered parameters, application authorization, anti-replay, ticket use, and deterministic errors.
Exporters and channel bindings enforce exact labels, contexts, transcript and version rules before releasing typed secret output.
The evergreen router selects one highest acceptable engine once and never retries or crosses transcript, credential, cache, PSK, ticket, or secret domains.
Multi-version routing requires cross-version, downgrade, transcript, separation, no-retry, interoperability, fuzz, and external-audit evidence.
Every TLS-family secret transition has explicit ownership, destruction, cancellation, and provider-failure behavior.
Version negotiation skips unknown offers, rejects recognized legacy versions, preserves transcript bytes, and selects one highest acceptable engine.
TLS 1.2 retains independent disablement and cannot pass its milestone without a separate external audit and clean remediation retest.
TLS and DTLS 1.2 never offer or select deprecated hashes, key exchange, certificate types, or imported forbidden state.
ECDHE ECDSA and RSA client and server handshakes are isolated, bounded, and entered only by the one-pass selector.
TLS 1.2 remains an isolated ECDHE-plus-AEAD engine that excludes obsolete protocol versions, algorithms, compression, renegotiation, and fallback.
Extended Main Secret is mandatory and binds the correct session hash, wire label, resumption consistency, indication, and failure behavior.
TLS 1.2 additions after the feature freeze fail closed except the exact authenticated security, ALPN, and exporter-label exceptions.
The TLS 1.2 PRF and key block enforce Extended Main Secret inputs, exact labels, domain separation, length limits, and secret destruction.
TLS 1.2 AEAD records enforce nonce, additional-data, sequence, record-limit, fragmentation, and failure-atomic open invariants.
TLS 1.2 resumption binds protocol-specific ticket state, extension hardening, downgrade behavior, lifetime, rotation, and interoperability.
TLS 1.2 owns version-specific SNI resumption binding, status_request negotiation, CertificateStatus handling, and safe unsupported ClientHello extension behavior.
Initial signaling cipher values and downgrade sentinels are context-checked while every subsequent renegotiation attempt is rejected.
The hardened TLS 1.2 profile admits exactly six reviewed ECDHE and AEAD combinations and rejects all other suites.
Alerts, close, illegal messages, backpressure, cancellation, and provider failure converge on deterministic terminal cleanup.
The TLS 1.3 engine cannot pass its milestone until an external audit and clean remediation retest cover its complete profile.
The server flight authenticates negotiation and certificates before application traffic while centralizing SNI and ALPN decisions.
Certificate negotiation applies signature, authority, OID-filter, public-key, resource, and deterministic external-signer constraints.
Client authentication, CertificateVerify, and Finished permit application traffic only after authenticated transcript verification.
ClientHello construction and parsing are bounded, preserve original transcript bytes, and apply SNI, ALPN, GREASE, padding, and offer policy.
TLS 1.3 conformance requires vectors, truncation, fragmentation, independent peers, state-model, fuzz, and provider-fault evidence.
Imported PSKs bind protocol, KDF, context, application, ALPN, and deployment domains and reject ambiguous or reused import state.
External PSKs remain distinct from resumption, require forward-secret modes, and fail without cross-profile fallback or identity ambiguity.
Provisioning enforces entropy, role, peer, node, identity, collision, privacy, rotation, and main-key destruction requirements.
Every TLS 1.3 handshake message and extension context has bounded canonical parsing, duplicate handling, ordering, and rejection behavior.
HelloRetryRequest enforces selected-group, cookie, second-ClientHello, message-hash, retry-count, and resource invariants.
KeyUpdate performs checked traffic-secret replacement, destroys obsolete keys immediately, and enforces request and record limits.
TLS 1.3 record protection validates inner plaintext and sequence exhaustion before committing any externally visible state.
The TLS 1.3 handshake state machine remains record-independent and has explicit stream, QUIC, and DTLS ownership boundaries.
All handshake effects are explicit deterministic actions with bounded input, output, provider, timer, cancellation, and terminal transitions.
Stateful tickets and binders use separated identity, cache, deployment, lifetime, concurrency, rotation, and constant-work failure domains.
Stateless ticket protection authenticates all protocol, identity, policy, timing, key-generation, and deployment-domain state.
Stapled OCSP and SCT bytes are bounded, context-checked, transcript-bound, and handed to admitted validation policy without interpretation drift.
The initial TLS 1.3 profile admits exactly the three reviewed AEAD and hash combinations and rejects every other suite.
Transcript and key-schedule transitions preserve exact bytes and destroy obsolete early, handshake, master, exporter, and resumption secrets.
Zero-RTT is opt-in and binds atomic anti-replay, freshness, ticket, storage, secret, rejection, and application side-effect policy.
